entities.name: Carnot Cycle
entities.description: Thermodynamic cycle consisting of four reversible steps: two isothermal and two adiabatic processes, operating between two thermal reservoirs at temperatures T₁ (hot) and T₂ (cold).

attributes.function: Idealized model for maximum thermodynamic efficiency

entities.name: Step A→B
entities.description: Isothermal expansion at hot reservoir temperature T₁. Gas absorbs heat and expands in piston-cylinder system.

attributes.position: Part (a), top-left; Part (b), upper isotherm from A to B; Part (c), top edge from A to B
attributes.function: Heat absorption from hot reservoir

entities.name: Step B→C
entities.description: Adiabatic expansion. Gas continues to expand without heat exchange, causing temperature to drop from T₁ to T₂.

attributes.position: Part (a), top-right to bottom-right; Part (b), upper-right adiabat from B to C; Part (c), right edge from B to C
attributes.function: Work output without heat transfer

entities.name: Step C→D
entities.description: Isothermal compression at cold reservoir temperature T₂. Gas releases heat while being compressed.

attributes.position: Part (a), bottom-right; Part (b), lower isotherm from C to D; Part (c), bottom edge from C to D
attributes.function: Heat rejection to cold reservoir

entities.name: Step D→A
entities.description: Adiabatic compression. Gas is compressed without heat exchange, raising temperature from T₂ back to T₁.

attributes.position: Part (a), bottom-left to top-left; Part (b), lower-left adiabat from D to A; Part (c), left edge from D to A
attributes.function: Work input to complete cycle

entities.name: Hot Reservoir (T₁)
entities.description: Thermal reservoir at high temperature T₁ that supplies heat during isothermal expansion (A→B).

attributes.function: Heat source for cycle

entities.name: Cold Reservoir (T₂)
entities.description: Thermal reservoir at low temperature T₂ that absorbs heat during isothermal compression (C→D).

attributes.function: Heat sink for cycle

entities.name: Piston-Cylinder System
entities.description: Mechanical system containing ideal gas, undergoing volume and pressure changes during the Carnot cycle.

attributes.function: Work interaction medium

entities.name: P-V Diagram
entities.description: Pressure-volume representation of the Carnot cycle showing two isotherms (A-B and C-D) and two adiabats (B-C and D-A).

attributes.function: Visualizes mechanical work as area enclosed by cycle
attributes.ocr_labels: Pressure, Volume, A, B, C, D, T₁, T₂

entities.name: T-S Diagram
entities.description: Temperature-entropy diagram forming a rectangle, with horizontal lines at T₁ and T₂ and vertical entropy changes during adiabatic steps.

attributes.function: Visualizes heat transfer as area under temperature-entropy curve

entities.name: Turbine Entry Temperature (TET)
entities.description: Operational take-off temperature at turbine entry in Rolls-Royce civil aeroengines, showing a continuous increase from approximately 1000 K in 1940 to over 1850 K by 2000, enabled by successive material and cooling innovations.

entities.name: Year
entities.description: Time period from 1940 to 2010 over which turbine entry temperature and material capability evolved.

entities.name: Material Capability
entities.description: Temperature capability of turbine blade materials, which increased in parallel with operational TET due to advancements including wrought alloys, cast alloys (conventional, directionally solidified (DS), single crystal (SC)), and thermal barrier coatings.

entities.name: Cooled Turbine Blades
entities.description: Key technological innovation enabling higher turbine entry temperatures by actively cooling blades, introduced during the mid-to-late 20th century as part of the TET evolution trend.

entities.name: Wrought Alloys
entities.description: Early high-temperature alloys used in turbine blades, contributing to initial TET increases from 1940s to 1950s, with capability up to ~1200 K.

entities.name: Cast Alloys
entities.description: Advanced nickel-based superalloys used in turbine blades, evolving from conventional casting to directionally solidified (DS) and single crystal (SC) forms, enabling TET increases beyond 1400 K from the 1960s onward.

entities.name: Thermal Barrier Coatings (TBCs)
entities.description: Ceramic coatings applied to turbine blades that insulate underlying superalloys, significantly enhancing effective temperature capability and enabling TETs above 1700 K from the 1980s onward.

entities.name: Rolls-Royce Civil Aeroengines
entities.description: Family of jet engines whose turbine entry temperature capability evolved from ~1000 K (1940) to >1850 K (2000), serving as real-world benchmarks for material and cooling technology progress.

relationships.description: Turbine Entry Temperature (TET) continuously increased with time from 1940 to 2000, rising from ~1000 K to over 1850 K.
relationships.source_sentence: The chart displays a continuous upward trend in both the operational Turbine Entry Temperature (TET) of engines and the temperature capability of materials from 1940 to 2010.

relationships.description: Material temperature capability increased in tandem with calendar year, driven by alloy and coating innovations.
relationships.source_sentence: The chart displays a continuous upward trend in both the operational Turbine Entry Temperature (TET) of engines and the temperature capability of materials from 1940 to 2010.

relationships.description: Wrought alloys enabled early increases in TET during the 1940s–1950s, supporting temperatures up to ~1150–1280 K.
relationships.source_sentence: The introduction of cooled turbine blades, wrought alloys, cast alloys (conventional, DS, SC), and thermal barrier coatings are marked as key technological advancements enabling this increase.

relationships.description: Cast superalloys—especially DS and SC variants—allowed TET to rise from ~1400 K (1965) to ~1700 K (1990s) by improving high-temperature creep and oxidation resistance.
relationships.source_sentence: The introduction of cooled turbine blades, wrought alloys, cast alloys (conventional, DS, SC), and thermal barrier coatings are marked as key technological advancements enabling this increase.

relationships.description: Thermal barrier coatings provided thermal insulation, enabling operational TET to exceed the melting point of underlying superalloys and reach >1800 K by the 1990s–2000s.
relationships.source_sentence: The introduction of cooled turbine blades, wrought alloys, cast alloys (conventional, DS, SC), and thermal barrier coatings are marked as key technological advancements enabling this increase.

relationships.description: Cooled turbine blades, using internal airflow to reduce metal temperature, decoupled operational TET from material melting limits and were critical for sustained TET growth post-1950s.
relationships.source_sentence: The introduction of cooled turbine blades, wrought alloys, cast alloys (conventional, DS, SC), and thermal barrier coatings are marked as key technological advancements enabling this increase.

relationships.description: Material capability closely tracks operational TET, indicating that engine performance is directly limited and enabled by available high-temperature materials.
relationships.source_sentence: The chart displays a continuous upward trend in both the operational Turbine Entry Temperature (TET) of engines and the temperature capability of materials from 1940 to 2010.

entities.name: Turbine Entry Temperature (TET)
entities.description: Temperature at the turbine inlet that varies significantly throughout a flight cycle, peaking during take-off and remaining elevated during climb, then stabilizing at a lower level during cruise, and further decreasing during approach and flight idle, with a brief spike during reverse thrust.

attributes.unit: °C (implied by context, though not explicitly stated)

entities.name: Time
entities.description: Duration of a typical civil aircraft flight cycle spanning 108 minutes, segmented into operational phases including ground idle, take-off, climb, cruise, approach, flight idle, reverse thrust, and return to ground idle.

entities.name: Take-off
entities.description: Initial high-power engine phase (0–2 min) where TET spikes to its maximum value, imposing peak thermal stress on turbine components.

entities.name: Climb
entities.description: Engine phase from 2 to 23 minutes where TET remains high but below take-off peak, sustaining significant thermal loading during aircraft ascent.

entities.name: Cruise
entities.description: Extended steady-state phase (23–86 min) where TET drops to a sustained, relatively stable level, representing the longest duration of thermal exposure during flight.

entities.name: Approach and Flight idle
entities.description: Phase from 86 to 107 minutes where TET decreases further as engine power is reduced for descent and landing preparation, resulting in lower thermal loading.

entities.name: Reverse thrust
entities.description: Brief post-landing phase causing a transient spike in TET due to engine reversal, introducing a secondary thermal shock after the main flight cycle.

entities.name: Ground idle
entities.description: Baseline engine state at start and end of flight cycle with minimal TET, representing low thermal stress condition before take-off and after landing.

entities.name: Thermal loading on engine components
entities.description: Highly variable thermal stress experienced by turbine materials due to cyclic TET changes during flight phases, with peak loading during take-off and secondary spike during reverse thrust.

relationships.description: TET exhibits a non-linear, phase-dependent variation over time during the flight cycle, with distinct thermal profiles corresponding to each operational phase.
relationships.source_sentence: The plot shows the Turbine Entry Temperature (TET) profile over a 108-minute flight.

relationships.description: During take-off (0–2 min), TET rapidly increases to its maximum value, representing the highest thermal demand of the flight cycle.
relationships.source_sentence: TET begins at 'Ground idle', spikes to its maximum during 'Take-off' (0-2 min)

relationships.description: After take-off, TET decreases slightly from its peak but remains high throughout the climb phase (2–23 min), indicating sustained but reduced thermal loading compared to take-off.
relationships.source_sentence: remains high during 'Climb' (2-23 min)

relationships.description: At the start of cruise (23 min), TET drops significantly from climb levels to a lower, sustained value that remains relatively constant for 63 minutes.
relationships.source_sentence: then drops to a sustained level for 'Cruise' (23-86 min)

attributes.magnitude: Substantial drop from climb to cruise level

relationships.description: During approach and flight idle (86–107 min), TET further decreases as engine power is reduced for landing, lowering thermal stress on components.
relationships.source_sentence: It decreases further for 'Approach' and 'Flight idle' (86-107 min)

relationships.description: Reverse thrust at landing induces a brief but sharp increase in TET, creating a secondary thermal transient after the main flight phases.
relationships.source_sentence: has a brief spike for 'Reverse thrust' upon landing

attributes.magnitude: Brief spike (lower than take-off peak, implied)

relationships.description: The cyclic variation in TET directly drives the thermal loading experienced by turbine engine components, with implications for material fatigue and lifespan.
relationships.source_sentence: This illustrates the highly variable thermal loading on engine components during a single flight.

entities.name: Turbojet Cycle
entities.description: Idealized thermodynamic cycle (1-3-4-9) for a turbojet engine depicted on a temperature-entropy diagram, assuming isentropic compression and expansion processes.

entities.name: Temperature
entities.description: Thermodynamic property plotted on the y-axis of the T-S diagram, representing the thermal state of the working fluid throughout the turbojet cycle stages.

entities.name: Entropy
entities.description: Thermodynamic property plotted on the x-axis of the T-S diagram, used to represent irreversibility; held constant during idealized isentropic compression (1-3) and expansion (4-9).

entities.name: Isentropic Compression
entities.description: Process 1-3 in the turbojet cycle where entropy remains constant (vertical line on T-S diagram) and temperature increases due to compression work (CW).

entities.name: Heat Addition
entities.description: Process 3-4 in the cycle where heat is added at constant pressure, shown as a diverging line from the origin on the T-S diagram, increasing both temperature and entropy.

entities.name: Isentropic Expansion
entities.description: Process 4-9 in the turbojet cycle where high-temperature gas expands through the turbine with constant entropy (vertical line), producing turbine work (TW) and decreasing temperature.

entities.name: Heat Rejection
entities.description: Process 9-1 where heat is rejected at constant pressure, returning the working fluid to its initial state along a line diverging from the origin on the T-S diagram.

entities.name: Compression Work (CW)
entities.description: Work input required for isentropic compression (1-3), represented as the area under the compression process on the T-S diagram.

entities.name: Turbine Work (TW)
entities.description: Work output from isentropic expansion (4-9) in the turbine, represented as the area under the expansion process on the T-S diagram.

entities.name: Useful Work (UW)
entities.description: Net work output of the turbojet cycle, defined as UW = TW - CW, representing the usable mechanical energy after accounting for compression work.

entities.name: Ideal Work of Combustion (Z)
entities.description: Theoretical maximum work obtainable from combustion process (3-4), labeled as Z on the diagram, corresponding to the heat addition at constant pressure.

entities.name: Turbojet Engine Cycle
entities.description: Thermodynamic cycle of a turbojet engine represented through P-V and T-S diagrams, comprising compression (1→3), heat addition/combustion (3→4), and expansion (4→9) processes.

entities.name: Pressure
entities.description: Pressure (p) in Pascals (Pa) plotted on the y-axis of diagram (a); increases during compression from point 1 to 3, peaks during combustion at point 4, and decreases during expansion to point 9.

entities.name: Volume
entities.description: Specific volume (V) in m³/kg plotted on the x-axis of diagram (a); decreases during compression (1→3), remains relatively constant or changes moderately during heat addition (3→4), and increases during expansion (4→9).

entities.name: Temperature
entities.description: Temperature (T) in Kelvin (K) plotted on the y-axis of diagram (b); rises during compression (1→3) and significantly increases during combustion (3→4), then decreases during expansion (4→9).

entities.name: Entropy
entities.description: Specific entropy (S) in J/kg·K plotted on the x-axis of diagram (b); increases during heat addition (3→4) due to fuel combustion, and may decrease or remain stable during expansion depending on process irreversibility.

entities.name: Compression Process (1→3)
entities.description: Thermodynamic phase in the turbojet cycle where working fluid is compressed, resulting in increased pressure and temperature, and decreased specific volume.

entities.name: Heat Addition / Combustion (3→4)
entities.description: Phase involving fuel injection and combustion, causing sharp rise in temperature and pressure; entropy increases due to irreversible heat addition.

entities.name: Expansion Process (4→9)
entities.description: Expansion of high-energy gas through turbine and nozzle, reducing pressure and temperature while increasing specific volume; entropy may remain constant (ideal) or increase (real).

entities.name: Fuel Input
entities.description: External energy source introduced between points 3 and 4, driving combustion and causing significant increases in temperature, pressure, and entropy.

entities.name: Activation energy for high-temperature creep
entities.description: Energy barrier required for high-temperature creep deformation, plotted on x-axis with values in kJ/mol. Shows strong positive correlation with self-diffusion activation energy across metals and ceramics, indicating diffusion-controlled creep mechanism.

entities.name: Activation energy for self-diffusion
entities.description: Energy barrier for atomic self-diffusion in solids, plotted on y-axis in kJ/mol. Closely matches creep activation energy values across materials, following a near 1:1 linear trend, supporting that creep is governed by diffusion kinetics.

entities.name: High-temperature creep
entities.description: Time-dependent plastic deformation at elevated temperatures, observed in various metals and ceramics. Its activation energy strongly correlates with self-diffusion energy, indicating a diffusion-controlled deformation mechanism.

entities.name: Self-diffusion
entities.description: Atomic migration process in pure materials where atoms exchange positions in the lattice. Its activation energy serves as a key indicator of creep behavior, as evidenced by the 1:1 correlation with creep activation energy.

entities.name: Metals and ceramics
entities.description: Class of materials (including both metals and ceramics) exhibiting a strong linear correlation between creep and self-diffusion activation energies, suggesting a universal diffusion-controlled creep mechanism across these material types.

entities.name: 1:1 correlation trend
entities.description: Observed linear trend where activation energy for self-diffusion approximately equals activation energy for high-temperature creep (slope ≈ 1), indicating that the rate-limiting step in creep is atomic diffusion.

relationships.description: Activation energy for high-temperature creep shows a strong positive linear correlation with activation energy for self-diffusion, closely following a 1:1 line across multiple materials.
relationships.source_sentence: The data points show a strong positive linear correlation, closely following a 1:1 line. This indicates that high-temperature creep is primarily a diffusion-controlled process in these materials.

entities.name: Primary dendrite arm spacing

entities.name: G⁻¹/²v⁻¹/⁴
entities.description: A dimensionless-like combined solidification parameter derived from the inverse square root of the temperature gradient (G) and the inverse fourth root of the withdrawal velocity (v), ranging from 0 to 0.4 m¹/⁴·s¹/⁴/K¹/², which strongly correlates with primary dendrite arm spacing across multiple superalloys.

entities.name: CMSX-4
entities.description: Single-crystal nickel-based superalloy whose phase fractions (γ, γ', liquid) vary with temperature; exhibits a solutioning window between 1300°C and 1350°C where only the γ phase is present.

entities.name: γ' phase
entities.description: Intermetallic strengthening phase in CMSX-4 that decreases steadily with temperature, from ~70 mol% at 400°C to 0 mol% at 1300°C, fully dissolving into the γ matrix within the solutioning window.

entities.name: γ phase
entities.description: FCC austenitic matrix phase in CMSX-4 that increases with temperature as γ' dissolves, reaching 100 mol% in the solutioning window (1300–1350°C) before liquid formation begins.

entities.name: Liquid phase
entities.description: Molten phase that appears above ~1350°C in CMSX-4 and becomes dominant above 1380°C, indicating the onset of melting beyond the solutioning window.

entities.name: Temperature
entities.description: Independent variable ranging from ~400°C to above 1380°C, controlling phase stability and transitions in CMSX-4, including γ' dissolution and liquid formation.

entities.name: Mole fraction
entities.description: Dependent variable representing the relative amount of each phase (γ, γ', liquid) in CMSX-4 as a function of temperature, normalized to sum to 1 at any given temperature.

entities.name: Solutioning window
entities.description: Narrow thermal processing window between 1300°C and 1350°C in CMSX-4 where the alloy consists entirely of the γ phase, critical for homogenization heat treatments without incipient melting.

relationships.description: The mole fraction of the γ' phase decreases monotonically with increasing temperature, from 0.7 at 400°C to 0 at 1300°C, due to thermal dissolution into the γ matrix.
relationships.source_sentence: As temperature increases, the γ' phase dissolves into the γ phase, with the γ' fraction decreasing to zero around 1300°C.

relationships.description: The mole fraction of the γ phase increases with temperature as γ' dissolves, rising from 0.3 at 400°C to 1.0 at 1300°C, maintaining 100% until liquid forms above 1350°C.
relationships.source_sentence: The material is fully γ phase in a narrow 'solutioning window' between roughly 1300°C and 1350°C.

relationships.description: The liquid phase mole fraction increases with temperature above ~1350°C, eventually reaching 1.0 above 1380°C, marking the onset and completion of melting.
relationships.source_sentence: Above this temperature, the liquid phase begins to form, and the alloy is fully liquid above approximately 1380°C.

relationships.description: CMSX-4 exhibits a solutioning window of approximately 50°C between 1300°C and 1350°C, where only the γ phase is stable.
relationships.source_sentence: Note the solutioning window of about 50 °C which lies between 1300°C and 1350°C.

relationships.description: Dissolution of the γ' phase directly increases the mole fraction of the γ phase, as γ' transforms into γ upon heating.
relationships.source_sentence: As temperature increases, the γ' phase dissolves into the γ phase...

entities.name: CMSX-4
entities.description: A nickel-based superalloy whose liquid density varies with temperature, showing a non-monotonic trend below the liquidus due to solute partitioning in the mushy zone.

entities.name: Liquid density
entities.description: Density of liquid CMSX-4 decreases overall with rising temperature, but exhibits a local minimum (~7.73 g/cm³ at 1625 K) in the mushy zone (below 1650 K) due to equilibrium solute partitioning, followed by a slight increase to 7.77 g/cm³ at the liquidus (1650 K), then a steady decline to 7.64 g/cm³ at 1800 K.

entities.name: Temperature
entities.description: Temperature range from 1550 K to 1800 K over which liquid CMSX-4 density is evaluated; below 1650 K corresponds to the mushy zone with equilibrium solute effects, above 1650 K represents fully liquid extrapolated behavior.

entities.name: Mushy zone liquid (equilibrium)
entities.description: Region below 1650 K where liquid CMSX-4 coexists with solid; density behavior accounts for solute partitioning under equilibrium assumptions, resulting in a non-monotonic density trend with a local minimum at ~1625 K.

entities.name: Extrapolated liquid (above liquidus)
entities.description: Extrapolated behavior of fully liquid CMSX-4 above 1650 K (up to 1800 K), showing a continuous density decrease from 7.77 to 7.64 g/cm³ with increasing temperature, based on reference [21].

entities.name: Local density minimum
entities.description: A local minimum in liquid density of ~7.73 g/cm³ observed at approximately 1625 K in the mushy zone, attributed to solute redistribution under equilibrium conditions.

relationships.description: Overall, liquid density of CMSX-4 decreases with increasing temperature from 1550 K to 1800 K, dropping from 7.83 to 7.64 g/cm³.
relationships.source_sentence: The plot shows that the density of liquid CMSX-4 generally decreases with increasing temperature.

relationships.description: Between 1550 K and 1650 K, liquid density in the mushy zone shows a non-monotonic trend: decreasing to a local minimum at 1625 K, then slightly increasing to 1650 K due to solute partitioning under equilibrium.
relationships.source_sentence: The solid line, representing the liquid in the mushy zone below 1650 K, shows a decrease from about 7.83 g/cm³ at 1550 K to a local minimum of about 7.73 g/cm³ around 1625 K, before slightly increasing to 7.77 g/cm³ at 1650 K.

entities.name: γ matrix
entities.description: Face-centered cubic (FCC) nickel-based matrix phase in single-crystal superalloys; its lattice parameter increases with temperature across all tested alloys (TMS63, TMS12, TMS19, CMSX-4), ranging approximately from 3.57 Å to 3.62 Å depending on alloy and temperature.

entities.name: γ' precipitates
entities.description: Ordered intermetallic L1₂ precipitate phase (Ni₃Al-type) in nickel-based superalloys; its lattice parameter increases with temperature in all four alloys, typically ranging from ~3.57 Å to ~3.63 Å, and exhibits alloy-dependent misfit relative to the γ matrix—e.g., consistently larger in CMSX-4 but crossing the γ line in TMS63.

entities.name: Temperature
entities.description: Independent variable in the chart, representing thermal conditions under which lattice parameters of γ and γ' phases were measured via X-ray diffraction; drives thermal expansion of both phases.

entities.name: Lattice parameter
entities.description: Crystallographic unit cell dimension measured in angstroms (Å); increases with temperature for both γ and γ' phases due to thermal expansion, with magnitude and relative behavior dependent on alloy composition.

entities.name: Lattice misfit
entities.description: Relative difference in lattice parameters between γ' precipitates and γ matrix; varies with temperature and alloy—changes sign in TMS63 (indicating a crossover point), remains positive in CMSX-4 (γ' > γ), and shows alloy-specific thermal evolution affecting coherency and strengthening.

entities.name: TMS63

entities.name: CMSX-4

entities.name: TMS12

entities.name: CMSX-4 superalloy

entities.name: Creep Strain

entities.name: Time
entities.description: Duration of creep testing in hours, spanning from 20 h to 280 h across both interrupted and rupture tests, used to track evolution of strain through primary, secondary, and tertiary creep stages.

entities.name: Rupture

entities.name: Interrupted Test
entities.description: Non-failure test condition represented by points A, B, and F, where specimens were removed before rupture to analyze microstructure or properties during creep; these occur at 20 h (0.5%), 110 h (1.0%), and 260 h (4.5%).

entities.name: Secondary Creep Plateau
entities.description: Steady-state creep phase with reproducible strain rate, observed between primary and tertiary stages; strain increases gradually from ~0.5% to ~2.2% over 20–200 h before acceleration into tertiary creep.

entities.name: Tertiary Creep Variability
entities.description: Final creep stage marked by accelerated strain and high scatter in rupture times (210–280 h) and strains (5.0–11.0%), indicating sensitivity to microstructural defects or local damage accumulation despite identical test conditions.

entities.name: Test Temperature
entities.description: Constant deformation temperature of 1150 °C during creep testing, a high fraction of the alloy’s melting point, promoting diffusion-mediated creep mechanisms and tertiary damage.

entities.name: PWA1480
entities.description: Nickel-based single-crystal superalloy exhibiting strong mechanical anisotropy; stress-strain response varies significantly with crystallographic orientation, showing trade-offs between strength and ductility.

entities.name: Stress
entities.description: Engineering stress (σ) measured in MPa, plotted on the y-axis; varies with strain and crystallographic orientation, with peak values corresponding to ultimate tensile strength before fracture.

entities.name: Strain
entities.description: Engineering strain (ε), dimensionless measure of deformation on the x-axis; ranges up to fracture strains between 0.116 and 0.256 depending on orientation.

entities.name: Fracture Strain 0.167
entities.description: Ductility metric for one crystallographic orientation of PWA1480, indicating failure occurs at strain ε = 0.167; associated with relatively high strength but moderate ductility.

entities.name: Fracture Strain 0.116
entities.description: Lowest observed ductility among tested orientations, with fracture at ε = 0.116; corresponds to a high-stiffness, high-yield-strength orientation.

entities.name: Fracture Strain 0.165
entities.description: Fracture strain value of ε = 0.165 for a specific crystallographic orientation, indicating moderate ductility similar to 0.167 case.

entities.name: Fracture Strain 0.256
entities.description: Highest ductility observed, with fracture at ε = 0.256; associated with a softer orientation exhibiting lower yield strength but greater plastic deformation capacity.

entities.name: Fracture Strain 0.219
entities.description: High ductility orientation fracturing at ε = 0.219; reflects a balance between strength and plasticity, superior to 0.16x cases but less than 0.256.

entities.name: Crystallographic Orientation
entities.description: Directional dependence of mechanical response in single-crystal PWA1480, sampled from the standard stereographic triangle; governs trade-off between yield strength and fracture strain.

entities.name: Mechanical Anisotropy
entities.description: Phenomenon where PWA1480 exhibits orientation-dependent stress-strain behavior: high-strength/low-ductility vs. low-strength/high-ductility responses across different crystallographic directions.

relationships.description: Crystallographic orientation strongly influences the stress response (including yield and ultimate tensile strength) of PWA1480 single crystals.
relationships.source_sentence: The curves demonstrate significant mechanical anisotropy. Some orientations exhibit high yield strength and stiffness but lower ductility, while others are softer (lower yield strength) but have greater fracture strains.

relationships.description: Fracture strain (maximum strain before failure) is highly dependent on crystallographic orientation, varying from 0.116 to 0.256.
relationships.source_sentence: Some orientations exhibit high yield strength and stiffness but lower ductility, while others are softer (lower yield strength) but have greater fracture strains.

relationships.description: Stress increases with strain in an orientation-dependent manner, following distinct stress-strain curves up to fracture points.
relationships.source_sentence: The chart presents a series of stress-strain curves for the PWA1480 superalloy, with each curve corresponding to a different crystallographic orientation.

relationships.description: PWA1480 single-crystal superalloy exhibits mechanical anisotropy due to its ordered crystal structure and orientation-sensitive slip systems.
relationships.source_sentence: The curves demonstrate significant mechanical anisotropy.

relationships.description: The orientation with fracture strain 0.116 corresponds to high stress (yield and ultimate) values, indicating a strong but brittle response.
relationships.source_sentence: Some orientations exhibit high yield strength and stiffness but lower ductility.

relationships.description: The orientation with fracture strain 0.256 shows lower stress levels (softer response) but sustains deformation to higher strains.
relationships.source_sentence: Others are softer (lower yield strength) but have greater fracture strains.

entities.name: Rene 95 superalloy
entities.description: Nickel-based superalloy tested in low-cycle fatigue at 650°C in three processing forms: extrusion and isothermal forging (EX+F), hot isostatic pressing (HIP), and cast-and-wrought (C&W). Exhibits processing-dependent fatigue performance, with EX+F showing superior life.

entities.name: Total strain range
entities.description: Total strain range (Δετ) measured in percent, plotted on the y-axis of a log-log fatigue curve. Ranges from approximately 0.4% to 2.0% based on typical low-cycle fatigue data; higher strain ranges lead to fewer cycles to failure across all material forms.

entities.name: Cycles to failure
entities.description: Number of cycles until fatigue failure (Nf), plotted on the x-axis on a logarithmic scale. Values span multiple orders of magnitude (e.g., ~10² to 10⁵ cycles); fatigue life increases as strain range decreases.

entities.name: EX+F (Extrusion and Isothermal Forging)
entities.description: Processing route for Rene 95 involving extrusion followed by isothermal forging. Demonstrates the highest fatigue resistance among the three forms: at any given Δετ, it achieves the highest Nf, indicating superior microstructural integrity and defect control.

entities.name: HIP (Hot Isostatic Pressing)
entities.description: Powder metallurgy processing route using hot isostatic pressing for Rene 95. Shows intermediate fatigue life between EX+F and C&W, suggesting effective pore closure but less optimized grain structure than EX+F.

entities.name: C&W (Cast-and-Wrought)
entities.description: Conventional cast-and-wrought form of Rene 95, exhibiting the shortest fatigue life at all strain ranges. Likely contains more microstructural heterogeneities or defects that accelerate crack initiation.

entities.name: Sub-surface failure
entities.description: Failure mode observed in fatigue testing where crack initiation occurs below the surface, possibly linked to internal defects such as inclusions or porosity. Noted in the legend as a distinct marker type.

entities.name: Test stopped
entities.description: Indicates fatigue tests that were terminated before failure occurred, possibly due to run-out criteria (e.g., exceeding a maximum cycle limit without fracture). Represented as censored data points.

entities.name: 650°C
entities.description: Testing temperature of 650°C, a high-temperature condition relevant to turbine engine applications, under which low-cycle fatigue behavior of Rene 95 was evaluated.

relationships.description: As total strain range (Δετ) increases, cycles to failure (Nf) decrease following a power-law trend typical of low-cycle fatigue, evident across all material forms on the log-log plot.
relationships.source_sentence: The chart plots total strain range (Δετ) versus cycles to failure (Nf) on a log-log scale...

attributes.magnitude: orders of magnitude reduction in Nf with increasing Δετ

relationships.description: EX+F processed Rene 95 exhibits the highest cycles to failure at any given strain range, indicating superior fatigue resistance compared to other processing routes.
relationships.source_sentence: The extruded and forged (EX+F) material shows the longest fatigue life...

relationships.description: HIP-processed Rene 95 shows intermediate fatigue life, with higher Nf than C&W but lower than EX+F at equivalent strain ranges.
relationships.source_sentence: ...followed by hot isostatic pressed (HIP), and finally conventional cast-and-wrought (C&W) material...

relationships.description: C&W Rene 95 has the lowest fatigue life, achieving the fewest cycles to failure at any given strain amplitude due to inferior microstructure.

entities.name: P/M superalloys
entities.description: Seven powder metallurgy (P/M) nickel-based superalloys with base composition Ni–11Cr–2.6Mo–3.8Ti–3.9Al–5.7W (wt%) and trace elements C (0.04), B (0.03), Zr (0.1); Nb (0–1), Ta (1–2), and Co (15–19) varied. Tested under dwell fatigue at 704 °C with 90 s hold and R = 0.1.

entities.name: Dwell fatigue crack propagation rate
entities.description: Crack growth rate (da/dt) under dwell fatigue conditions at 704 °C with 90 s hold time and stress ratio R = 0.1. Ranges over approximately one order of magnitude lower in super-solvus vs. sub-solvus processed alloys across stress intensities from ~15 to 40 MPa·m¹/².

entities.name: Maximum stress intensity
entities.description: Applied stress intensity factor (K_max) during dwell fatigue testing, ranging approximately from 15 to 40 MPa·m¹/². Serves as the driving force for crack propagation in the log-log plot.

entities.name: Sub-solvus processing
entities.description: Heat treatment condition where the alloy is processed below the solvus temperature of the γ' phase, resulting in a finer microstructure and higher dwell fatigue crack propagation rates—approximately 10× higher than super-solvus counterparts across the tested stress intensity range.

entities.name: Super-solvus processing
entities.description: Heat treatment condition where the alloy is processed above the γ' solvus temperature, leading to a coarse, homogenized microstructure that significantly improves dwell fatigue resistance—reducing crack propagation rates by about an order of magnitude compared to sub-solvus processing.

entities.name: Test temperature

entities.name: Udimet 710

entities.name: γ' phase

entities.name: γ" phase

entities.name: Astroloy
entities.description: Nickel-based superalloy studied for fatigue crack propagation behavior at room temperature under cyclic loading (R = 0.1, 40 Hz). Exhibits distinct crack growth responses depending on crack length and grain size.

entities.name: Fatigue Crack Propagation Rate
entities.description: Measured as da/dN (mm/cycle), this property quantifies how quickly a fatigue crack advances per loading cycle. For Astroloy at room temperature, short cracks propagate faster than long cracks at identical ΔK; short cracks also grow below the long-crack threshold ΔK.

entities.name: Stress Intensity Factor Range
entities.description: Denoted as ΔK (MPa m¹/²), this driving force for crack growth is plotted on the x-axis. Crack propagation rates increase with ΔK, but short cracks in Astroloy exhibit growth even below the apparent threshold ΔK for long cracks.

entities.name: Fine-Grained Astroloy
entities.description: Astroloy with fine grain structure (FG). For long cracks, shows slightly faster propagation than coarse-grained material; for short cracks, grain size effect is minimal and propagation remains rapid.

entities.name: Coarse-Grained Astroloy
entities.description: Astroloy with coarse grain structure (CG). Exhibits marginally slower long-crack propagation compared to fine-grained counterpart, but negligible difference in short-crack behavior.

entities.name: Long Crack
entities.description: Crack length sufficient to be governed by linear elastic fracture mechanics. In Astroloy, long cracks propagate slower than short cracks at the same ΔK and exhibit a measurable threshold ΔK below which growth does not occur.

entities.name: Short Crack
entities.description: Crack length small relative to microstructural features (e.g., grain size). In Astroloy, short cracks propagate faster than long cracks at identical ΔK, grow below the long-crack threshold ΔK, and show minimal sensitivity to grain size.

entities.name: Room Temperature
entities.description: Testing condition at ambient temperature (~25°C), under which fatigue crack propagation data for Astroloy were collected at R = 0.1 and 40 Hz.

entities.name: Load Ratio R = 0.1

entities.name: Frequency 40 Hz
entities.description: Cyclic loading frequency of 40 Hz applied during fatigue crack propagation tests on Astroloy at room temperature.

entities.name: Reduced Grain Size Effect for Short Cracks
entities.description: Observation that grain size (fine vs. coarse) has minimal influence on fatigue crack propagation rate when cracks are short, in contrast to long cracks where coarse grains slightly retard growth.

entities.name: Short-Crack Acceleration
entities.description: Phenomenon where short cracks in Astroloy propagate faster than long cracks at the same ΔK, and can grow below the nominal threshold ΔK for long cracks.

entities.name: Turbine disc alloys
entities.description: High-performance nickel-based superalloys used in turbine discs, whose mechanical properties exhibit a trade-off behavior depending on grain size, requiring optimization for specific service conditions.

entities.name: Grain size
entities.description: Microstructural feature measured in micrometers (µm) that critically influences mechanical performance: smaller grain sizes enhance tensile strength and low-cycle fatigue life but reduce creep strength and dwell crack growth resistance.

entities.name: Tensile strength
entities.description: Normalized strength metric that decreases with increasing grain size in turbine disc alloys, reflecting the Hall-Petch strengthening mechanism at finer grain scales.

entities.name: Low-cycle fatigue (LCF) life
entities.description: Normalized fatigue life under high-strain cyclic loading that decreases as grain size increases, indicating better fatigue resistance in fine-grained microstructures.

entities.name: Creep strength
entities.description: Normalized resistance to time-dependent deformation at high temperatures that increases with larger grain size due to reduced grain boundary sliding in coarse-grained turbine disc alloys.

entities.name: Dwell crack growth resistance
entities.description: Normalized resistance to crack propagation during stress dwell periods that improves with increasing grain size, suggesting coarse grains mitigate dwell-sensitive cracking mechanisms.

relationships.description: As grain size increases, tensile strength decreases, consistent with Hall-Petch behavior where finer grains impede dislocation motion more effectively.
relationships.source_sentence: Tensile strength and LCF (low-cycle fatigue) life decrease as grain size increases.

relationships.description: LCF life decreases with increasing grain size, indicating that fine-grained microstructures provide superior resistance to fatigue crack initiation under cyclic loading.
relationships.source_sentence: Tensile strength and LCF (low-cycle fatigue) life decrease as grain size increases.

relationships.description: Creep strength increases with grain size due to fewer grain boundaries available for diffusion-mediated deformation mechanisms like grain boundary sliding.
relationships.source_sentence: Creep strength and resistance to dwell crack growth increase with increasing grain size.

relationships.description: Resistance to dwell crack growth improves with larger grain size, likely because coarse grains reduce susceptibility to environmentally assisted or time-dependent intergranular cracking during stress holds.
relationships.source_sentence: Creep strength and resistance to dwell crack growth increase with increasing grain size.

relationships.description: Turbine disc alloys exhibit grain size as a key microstructural parameter that governs the trade-off among competing mechanical properties.

entities.description: Crack propagation rate measured in mm/s under dwell fatigue conditions (90 s hold, R = 0.1) at 704 °C; ranges from lowest in furnace-cooled condition (a) to highest in sub-solvus resolutioned condition (c), indicating strong sensitivity to γ' microstructure.

entities.name: Maximum stress intensity

entities.name: ASTM 8.5 grain size

entities.name: -3σ curve

entities.name: Predicted safe cycle life (Ar)

entities.name: Assumed location of test component

entities.name: Predicted Fatigue Life
entities.description: Number of cycles to failure (Np) predicted based on flaw size and inclusion diameter; increases exponentially as normalised flaw size (d/D) approaches 0 and drops to zero as d/D approaches 1. Larger inclusions consistently yield lower Np values across all normalised flaw sizes.

entities.name: Normalised Flaw Size
entities.description: Ratio of flaw size (d) to inclusion diameter (D), denoted d/D; ranges from near 0 (small flaw relative to inclusion) to 1 (flaw equals full inclusion diameter). Governs exponential variation in predicted fatigue life.

entities.name: Inclusion Diameter 10 µm
entities.description: Inclusion with diameter D = 10 µm; yields the highest predicted fatigue life among all inclusion sizes at any given normalised flaw size (d/D), reflecting reduced susceptibility to fatigue failure compared to larger inclusions.

entities.name: Inclusion Diameter 20 µm
entities.description: Inclusion with diameter D = 20 µm; exhibits lower predicted fatigue life than 10 µm inclusions but higher than 30 µm and 90 µm inclusions across all normalised flaw sizes.

entities.name: Inclusion Diameter 30 µm
entities.description: Inclusion with diameter D = 30 µm; shows reduced predicted fatigue life compared to smaller inclusions (10 µm, 20 µm) at all normalised flaw sizes, indicating greater fatigue sensitivity.

entities.name: Inclusion Diameter 90 µm
entities.description: Inclusion with diameter D = 90 µm; consistently yields the lowest predicted fatigue life across all normalised flaw sizes, demonstrating that larger inclusions drastically reduce fatigue resistance.

relationships.description: As normalised flaw size (d/D) increases toward 1, predicted fatigue life (Np) decreases sharply to zero, indicating that flaws approaching the full inclusion diameter cause immediate fatigue failure.
relationships.source_sentence: as the flaw size approaches the full inclusion diameter (d/D -> 1), the predicted life drops to zero

relationships.description: As normalised flaw size (d/D) approaches zero, predicted fatigue life increases exponentially, reflecting high fatigue resistance when flaws are much smaller than the inclusion.
relationships.source_sentence: the predicted life increases exponentially as the normalised flaw size approaches zero

relationships.description: Larger inclusion diameter (90 µm) results in consistently lower predicted fatigue life compared to smaller inclusions at any given normalised flaw size, indicating that inclusion size negatively impacts fatigue performance.
relationships.source_sentence: Curves for larger inclusion diameters (e.g., 90 m) are consistently lower than those for smaller diameters (e.g., 10 m), indicating a shorter fatigue life for larger inclusions at any given normalised flaw size.

entities.name: Rotating Disc with Central Hole
entities.description: A uniform rotating disc with outer radius b and a central hole of radius a; exhibits distinct radial and hoop stress distributions where hoop stress peaks at the inner radius and radial stress peaks internally while being zero at both boundaries.

entities.name: Solid Rotating Disc
entities.description: A uniform rotating disc with no central hole (a = 0); both radial and hoop stresses attain their maximum values at the center (r = 0) and decrease radially outward.

entities.name: Hoop Stress (σθ)
entities.description: Circumferential stress in the rotating disc; in a disc with a central hole, it is maximum at the inner radius 'a' and decreases monotonically toward the outer radius 'b'; in a solid disc (a=0), it is highest at the center and decreases outward.

entities.name: Radial Stress (σr)
entities.description: Radially directed stress in the rotating disc; for a disc with a central hole, it is zero at both inner radius 'a' and outer radius 'b', reaching a maximum at an intermediate radial location; in a solid disc, it peaks at the center and decreases outward.

entities.name: Radial Distance
entities.description: Distance from the center of the disc, ranging from inner radius 'a' (or 0 for solid disc) to outer radius 'b'; serves as the independent variable governing stress distribution.

entities.name: Central Hole Radius (a)
entities.description: Radius of the central hole in the disc; when a > 0, stress distributions differ significantly from solid disc case; when a = 0, disc is solid and stresses peak at center.

entities.name: Outer Radius (b)
entities.description: Fixed outer boundary of the disc; radial stress is zero at r = b for both solid and holed configurations.

relationships.description: In a disc with a central hole (a > 0), hoop stress (σθ) decreases with increasing radial distance from the inner radius 'a' to the outer radius 'b'.
relationships.source_sentence: The hoop stress (σθ) is maximum at the inner radius 'a' and decreases towards the outer radius 'b'.

relationships.description: Radial stress (σr) in a holed disc correlates non-monotonically with radial distance: it starts at zero at r = a, rises to a peak at an intermediate radius, then falls back to zero at r = b.
relationships.source_sentence: The radial stress (σr) is zero at both the inner and outer radii and peaks somewhere in between.

relationships.description: Presence of a central hole (a > 0) shifts the location of maximum hoop stress from the center (r=0) to the inner boundary (r=a), fundamentally altering stress distribution compared to solid disc.
relationships.source_sentence: The dashed lines show the stress distribution for a solid disc (a=0), where both stresses are maximum at the center.

relationships.source_sentence: The dashed lines show the stress distribution for a solid disc (a=0), where both stresses are maximum at the center.

entities.name: Nucleation
entities.description: Initial stage of fatigue crack failure where crack size is minimal and no significant growth is observed; occurs at the beginning of material life.

entities.name: Short crack growth
entities.description: Intermediate fatigue stage characterized by small, step-like increases in crack size over material life; precedes rapid crack propagation.

entities.name: Crack growth defined by K
entities.description: Final pre-fracture stage where crack size increases at an accelerating, exponential rate governed by stress intensity factor (K) until final fracture occurs.

entities.name: Final fracture
entities.description: Terminal failure event triggered when crack size reaches critical length governed by material fracture toughness; marks end of fatigue life.

entities.name: Crack size
entities.description: Measure of crack length that evolves through distinct fatigue stages: remains near zero during nucleation, increases step-wise during short crack growth, and accelerates exponentially in the K-governed propagation phase until final fracture.

entities.name: Life
entities.description: Cumulative fatigue cycles or time over which crack evolution occurs, segmented into nucleation, short crack growth, and rapid propagation phases.

entities.name: Fracture toughness
entities.description: Material property that governs the onset of final fracture when crack size reaches a critical value; determines the endpoint of the fatigue life curve.

entities.name: Stress intensity factor (K)
entities.description: Parameter controlling the exponential crack growth rate in the final propagation stage; denoted by 'K' in the phase 'Crack growth defined by K'.

relationships.description: Crack size evolves non-linearly with life: initially stable, then step-wise, then exponentially increasing.
relationships.source_sentence: The chart illustrates the progression of crack size over the life of a material.

relationships.description: During nucleation, crack size remains minimal with negligible growth.
relationships.source_sentence: The process begins with a 'Nucleation' phase where crack size is minimal.

relationships.description: Short crack growth phase shows small, step-like increases in crack size over life.
relationships.source_sentence: This is followed by a 'Short crack growth' phase, characterized by small, step-like increases in crack size.

relationships.description: Crack growth defined by K exhibits accelerating, exponential increase in crack size until final fracture.
relationships.source_sentence: The final stage is 'Crack growth defined by K', where the crack grows at an accelerating, exponential rate until 'Final fracture'.

relationships.description: Final fracture is governed by the material's fracture toughness, which determines the critical crack size for failure.
relationships.source_sentence: Final fracture governed by the fracture toughness.

relationships.description: Stress intensity factor (K) governs the exponential crack growth behavior in the final propagation stage.
relationships.source_sentence: Crack growth defined by K

entities.name: Dwell fatigue crack growth rate

entities.name: Rene 95

entities.name: Astroloy

entities.name: MERL 76
entities.description: A P/M superalloy following the typical correlation between high yield stress and elevated dwell fatigue crack growth rate at 650°C.

entities.name: N18
entities.description: A P/M superalloy specifically engineered to achieve high 0.2% yield stress while maintaining a low dwell fatigue crack growth rate, deviating favorably from the general trend and located in a highlighted target region.

entities.name: 650°C

entities.name: General trend: yield stress increases with crack growth rate

entities.name: N18 target region deviation

Values increase with B, Zr, or Hf additions compared to Alloy 1 and CW U720, with Alloy 4 (likely containing one or more of these elements) showing the highest improvement at 425°C in ASTM 11 grain size.

entities.name: Rene 95
entities.description: Nickel-based superalloy Rene 95, whose probabilistic failure behavior is analyzed under cyclic loading. Larger volumes of this material exhibit higher failure probabilities at a given number of cycles compared to smaller volumes or specimens.

entities.name: Probability of failure
entities.description: The likelihood that Rene 95 fails under cyclic loading, ranging from near 0% at low cycle counts to approaching 100% at high cycle counts. Exhibits an S-shaped trend with number of cycles and is strongly influenced by component volume.

entities.name: Number of cycles
entities.description: The number of loading cycles (No) applied to Rene 95, normalized by 1000 (i.e., No/1000). Serves as the independent variable against which failure probability is evaluated, with higher values leading to increased failure likelihood.

entities.name: Large volume

entities.name: Small volume
entities.description: A test condition representing a smaller component volume of Rene 95. Exhibits intermediate fatigue life and failure probability between 'Large volume' and 'Specimen'.

entities.name: Specimen
entities.description: A standard test specimen of Rene 95 with the smallest effective volume. Demonstrates the longest fatigue life and lowest failure probability at a given number of cycles due to reduced defect likelihood.

entities.name: S-shaped failure probability curve
entities.description: Characteristic sigmoidal trend in failure probability vs. cycle count for Rene 95, indicating low initial failure risk, rapid increase in mid-life, and saturation near 100% at high cycles. Observed across all volume conditions.

relationships.description: The probability of failure increases with the number of cycles, following an S-shaped curve for all volume conditions of Rene 95.

entities.name: Udimet 720
entities.description: Powder metallurgy nickel-based superalloy Udimet 720, tested under low cycle fatigue (LCF) conditions with varying inclusion sizes and stress ratios (R = -1, 0, 0.5).

entities.name: Low Cycle Fatigue (LCF) Life
entities.description: Number of life cycles to failure under cyclic strain loading; ranges across multiple orders of magnitude on a log scale. Unseeded material exhibits the highest LCF life, while life decreases with increasing inclusion size (54 µm → 122 µm) at all R ratios.

entities.name: Strain Range
entities.description: Applied cyclic strain amplitude in LCF testing, plotted on a logarithmic scale in units of mm/mm (dimensionless). Higher strain ranges correspond to shorter fatigue lives across all material conditions.

entities.name: Unseeded Condition
entities.description: Baseline condition of Udimet 720 without artificially introduced inclusions; exhibits the longest LCF life across all R ratios (-1, 0, 0.5) at any given strain range.

entities.name: 54 µm Inclusions
entities.description: Artificially seeded inclusions of 54 micrometer diameter in Udimet 720; reduce LCF life compared to unseeded material but less severely than 122 µm inclusions, consistently across R = -1, 0, and 0.5.

entities.name: 122 µm Inclusions
entities.description: Artificially seeded inclusions of 122 micrometer diameter in Udimet 720; cause the greatest reduction in LCF life among tested conditions, resulting in the shortest fatigue life at all R ratios and strain ranges.

entities.name: Stress Ratio R = -1

entities.name: Stress Ratio R = 0
entities.description: Fatigue test condition with zero-to-tension loading (R = 0); exhibits same trend as R = -1: LCF life decreases with larger inclusion size.

entities.name: Stress Ratio R = 0.5
entities.description: Fatigue test condition with tensile mean stress (R = 0.5); continues the consistent trend: unseeded material outperforms seeded variants, and 122 µm inclusions yield shortest life.

entities.description: Size of inclusions (in micrometers) that act as failure-initiating defects in Rene 95 under 1000 MPa stress; peak failure probability shifts to larger sizes (100–450 µm) with increasing component volume.

entities.name: Probability, inclusion initiating failure
entities.description: Probability (scaled by 10⁻³) that a given inclusion size initiates failure in Rene 95 at a fixed overall failure probability of 1% (p3 = 0.01) and 1000 MPa stress; exhibits bell-shaped distributions with peaks dependent on component geometry.

entities.name: Specimen
entities.description: Smallest component geometry in the probabilistic model; exhibits peak failure-initiating inclusion probability at ~100 µm, indicating highest sensitivity to smaller inclusions compared to larger geometries.

entities.name: Small volume
entities.description: Intermediate component geometry; most likely to fail due to inclusions around 300 µm, showing a rightward shift in peak failure probability compared to 'Specimen'.

entities.name: Large volume
entities.description: Largest component geometry; peak failure-initiating inclusion size is ~450 µm, demonstrating increased susceptibility to larger, rarer inclusions due to greater material volume.

entities.name: Applied stress
entities.description: Constant applied stress of 1000 MPa used in the probabilistic failure model for Rene 95 across all component geometries.

entities.name: Overall failure probability (p3)
entities.description: Fixed overall failure probability of 0.01 (1%) used as a constraint in the probabilistic model to compute inclusion-initiated failure probabilities (p4) across geometries.

entities.name: Bell-shaped failure probability distribution
entities.description: Characteristic trend in all three geometries where the probability of inclusion-initiated failure rises to a peak and then declines with increasing inclusion size, with peak location dependent on component volume.

relationships.description: The 'Specimen' geometry exhibits peak failure-initiating inclusion probability at approximately 100 µm inclusion size.

entities.name: 80% confidence limit

entities.name: yttria-stabilised zirconia (7YSZ)
entities.description: A ceramic material (7 mol% yttria-stabilized zirconia) whose thermal conductivity decreases with rising temperature and is significantly reduced by smaller grain sizes, especially below 1000 °C.

entities.name: Thermal conductivity
entities.description: Thermal conductivity of 7YSZ decreases with increasing temperature across all grain sizes, ranging from ~2.5 W/(m·K) (Intrinsic, 25 °C) down to ~1.0 W/(m·K) (5 nm, 25 °C), and converges to ~1.2–1.4 W/(m·K) near 1200 °C regardless of grain size.

entities.name: Temperature
entities.description: Temperature ranges from ambient (~25 °C) to 1200 °C; as temperature increases, thermal conductivity of 7YSZ consistently decreases for all grain sizes, with grain size effects diminishing above ~1000 °C.

entities.name: Intrinsic grain size
entities.description: Represents the theoretical upper limit of thermal conductivity in 7YSZ with negligible grain boundary scattering; exhibits the highest thermal conductivity across all temperatures, decreasing from ~2.5 W/(m·K) at 25 °C to ~1.4 W/(m·K) at 1200 °C.

entities.name: 1 μm grain size
entities.description: 7YSZ with 1 micrometer grain size shows slightly reduced thermal conductivity compared to intrinsic, with a similar decreasing trend with temperature and partial convergence toward other grain sizes above 1000 °C.

entities.name: 100 nm grain size
entities.description: Nanocrystalline 7YSZ with 100 nm grains exhibits notably lower thermal conductivity than larger grain sizes at low temperatures, but the difference narrows above 800–1000 °C as curves begin to converge.

entities.name: 50 nm grain size
entities.description: 7YSZ with 50 nm grains shows further reduction in thermal conductivity, especially below 600 °C, contributing to strong grain boundary phonon scattering that weakens at elevated temperatures.

entities.name: 10 nm grain size
entities.description: Ultrafine-grained 7YSZ (10 nm) displays very low thermal conductivity at room temperature (~1.1–1.2 W/(m·K)), with a shallow decline as temperature rises, approaching the 5 nm curve at high T.

entities.name: 5 nm grain size
entities.description: The smallest grain size (5 nm) yields the lowest thermal conductivity in 7YSZ across all temperatures, starting near ~1.0 W/(m·K) at 25 °C and showing minimal further reduction with heating, nearly merging with other nanograined curves by 1200 °C.

entities.name: Grain boundary scattering
entities.description: Phonon scattering at grain boundaries in nanocrystalline 7YSZ suppresses thermal conductivity, with effectiveness diminishing at high temperatures (>1000 °C) due to dominant intrinsic phonon-phonon scattering.

entities.name: Convergence of thermal conductivity at high temperature
entities.description: Above ~1000–1200 °C, thermal conductivity curves for all grain sizes converge to similar values (~1.2–1.4 W/(m·K)), indicating that intrinsic thermal resistance dominates over grain boundary effects.

relationships.description: Thermal conductivity of 7YSZ decreases as temperature increases for all grain sizes due to enhanced phonon-phonon Umklapp scattering.
relationships.source_sentence: Thermal conductivity decreases with increasing temperature for all conditions.

attributes.magnitude: Approximately 30–60% reduction from 25 °C to 1200 °C depending on grain size

relationships.description: Grain boundary scattering in nanocrystalline 7YSZ reduces thermal conductivity, with impact most significant at low temperatures where phonon mean free path exceeds grain size.
relationships.source_sentence: The effect of grain size is most pronounced at lower temperatures, with the curves converging at higher temperatures around 1200 °C.

relationships.description: At high temperatures (~1200 °C), increasing temperature causes all grain size variants to exhibit nearly identical thermal conductivity, indicating dominance of intrinsic scattering mechanisms.
relationships.source_sentence: The effect of grain size is most pronounced at lower temperatures, with the curves converging at higher temperatures around 1200 °C.

relationships.description: 10 nm grain size significantly lowers thermal conductivity relative to coarser microstructures, particularly below 800 °C.

entities.name: Erbia-doped zirconia coating
entities.description: Zirconia-based coating doped with 4 mol% Erbia (Er₂O₃), exhibiting reduced thermal conductivity of 1.3 W/(m K) at room temperature compared to the undoped reference, indicating moderate phonon scattering enhancement.

entities.name: Ytterbia-doped zirconia coating
entities.description: Zirconia-based coating doped with 4 mol% Ytterbia (Yb₂O₃), showing significantly reduced thermal conductivity of 0.9 W/(m K) at room temperature, reflecting strong lattice distortion and phonon scattering.

entities.name: Neodymia-doped zirconia coating
entities.description: Zirconia-based coating doped with 4 mol% Neodymia (Nd₂O₃), with thermal conductivity of 0.95 W/(m K) at room temperature, demonstrating substantial reduction due to enhanced point defect scattering.

entities.name: Gadolinia-doped zirconia coating
entities.description: Zirconia-based coating doped with 4 mol% Gadolinia (Gd₂O₃), achieving the lowest thermal conductivity of 0.85 W/(m K) at room temperature among all tested dopants, indicating optimal mass and strain contrast for phonon scattering.

entities.name: Thermal conductivity

entities.name: VJL12U superalloy
entities.description: Nickel-based superalloy tested under low-cycle-fatigue (LCF) conditions at 20°C in three surface conditions: uncoated, aluminised coating, and Ni-20Cr-12Al-Y overlay coating.

entities.name: Strain
entities.description: Total strain (ε) expressed as a percentage, plotted on a logarithmic scale against number of cycles to failure; ranges from approximately 0.2% to 2% based on typical LCF behavior shown in the trend.

entities.name: Number of cycles
entities.description: Number of load cycles to failure (N), plotted on a logarithmic scale; fatigue life varies significantly with coating type, with uncoated showing the highest N and Ni-20Cr-12Al-Y coated the lowest.

entities.name: Uncoated condition
entities.description: Baseline surface condition of VJL12U superalloy with no coating; exhibits the longest low-cycle-fatigue life at 20°C among the three tested conditions.

entities.name: Aluminised coating
entities.description: Surface coating applied to VJL12U superalloy that slightly reduces low-cycle-fatigue life compared to the uncoated condition at 20°C.

entities.name: Ni-20Cr-12Al-Y overlay coating
entities.description: Overlay coating composed of nickel with 20% chromium, 12% aluminum, and yttrium; causes the most significant reduction in low-cycle-fatigue life of VJL12U superalloy at 20°C.

entities.name: Test temperature
entities.description: Low-cycle-fatigue tests conducted at 20°C, a room-temperature condition that serves as the environmental parameter for all three coating comparisons.

entities.name: Fatigue life reduction trend
entities.description: Observed degradation in fatigue life (N) with coating application: uncoated > aluminised > Ni-20Cr-12Al-Y, indicating that coating-induced embrittlement or stress concentration worsens with more complex overlay systems at 20°C.

entities.name: JS6U superalloy
entities.description: Nickel-based superalloy tested for creep rupture behavior at 800°C and 900°C under various environmental and coating conditions.

entities.name: Stress
entities.description: Applied stress (σ) during creep rupture testing, plotted on the y-axis in MPa. Higher stress leads to shorter rupture times; values span a range typical for superalloy creep testing on a log scale.

entities.name: Time to rupture
entities.description: Duration until specimen failure under constant stress and temperature, measured in hours. Exhibits inverse logarithmic relationship with stress; significantly reduced by synthetic ash exposure in uncoated samples.

entities.name: No coating, in air
entities.description: Baseline test condition for JS6U superalloy at 800°C and 900°C in air without any protective coating, showing the highest rupture life among uncoated conditions.

entities.name: No coating, in ash
entities.description: JS6U superalloy exposed to synthetic ash at 800°C and 900°C without coating, resulting in significantly reduced time to rupture compared to air exposure due to environmental degradation.

entities.name: Coating Al-5Si-1.5Y, in ash
entities.description: Aluminum-silicon-yttrium alloy coating applied to JS6U superalloy, tested in synthetic ash at 800°C and 900°C. Provides partial protection against ash-induced degradation, improving rupture life over uncoated-in-ash but less effective than Ni-based coating.

entities.name: Coating Ni-20Co-20Cr-12Al-Yr, in ash
entities.description: Nickel-cobalt-chromium-aluminum-yttrium overlay coating applied to JS6U superalloy, tested in synthetic ash at 800°C and 900°C. Restores creep rupture life to levels comparable to or exceeding the uncoated alloy in air, indicating high resistance to ash-induced damage.

entities.name: Synthetic ash
entities.description: Corrosive environmental condition applied during testing that drastically reduces creep rupture life of uncoated JS6U superalloy at both 800°C and 900°C.

entities.name: Temperature = 800°C
entities.description: Test temperature at which creep rupture curves were generated; used in conjunction with 900°C to evaluate temperature dependence of coating performance in ash and air.

entities.name: Temperature = 900°C
entities.description: Higher test temperature used to assess accelerated creep and environmental degradation effects; trends similar to 800°C but with generally reduced rupture times.

entities.name: Ni–15Cr–13Al
entities.description: Base NiCrAl alloy (Ni–15Cr–13Al) without dopants, exhibiting poor Al2O3 scale adherence during cyclic oxidation at 1100 °C, as evidenced by continuous and significant weight loss due to scale spallation.

entities.name: Ni–15Cr–13Al + 0.5 wt% Yttrium
entities.description: NiCrAl alloy doped with 0.5 wt% yttrium, showing excellent Al2O3 scale adherence during 1100 °C cyclic oxidation (1 h cycles), with only a small initial weight gain followed by stable weight change, indicating minimal spallation.

entities.name: Ni–15Cr–13Al + 0.5 wt% Zirconium
entities.description: NiCrAl alloy doped with 0.5 wt% zirconium, demonstrating excellent Al2O3 scale adherence under 1100 °C cyclic oxidation (1 h cycles), with a small initial weight gain and subsequent stable or very slightly increasing weight, indicating strong scale retention.

entities.name: Weight change
entities.description: Measure of oxidation-induced mass change per unit area (mg/cm²), used to assess scale adherence; negative values indicate spallation (weight loss), while stable or slightly positive values indicate protective, adherent Al2O3 scale.

entities.name: Oxidation time
entities.description: Duration of cyclic oxidation exposure, measured in 1-hour cycles at 1100 °C, used to evaluate long-term scale stability and adherence behavior.

entities.name: Al2O3 scale adherence
entities.description: The ability of the thermally grown Al2O3 oxide scale to remain bonded to the NiCrAl alloy substrate during thermal cycling; poor adherence leads to spallation (weight loss), while good adherence results in stable weight gain.

entities.name: Yttrium dopant
entities.description: 0.5 wt% yttrium added to Ni–15Cr–13Al to improve Al2O3 scale adherence by reducing spallation during cyclic oxidation at 1100 °C.

entities.name: Zirconium dopant
entities.description: 0.5 wt% zirconium added to Ni–15Cr–13Al to enhance Al2O3 scale adherence, resulting in minimal weight change during cyclic oxidation at 1100 °C.

entities.name: Cyclic oxidation test at 1100 °C
entities.description: High-temperature oxidation environment involving repeated 1-hour heating/cooling cycles at 1100 °C, used to assess thermal barrier coating or scale durability through spallation resistance.

relationships.description: Undoped Ni–15Cr–13Al exhibits continuous weight loss (negative weight change) with increasing oxidation time, indicating progressive Al2O3 scale spallation due to poor adherence.
relationships.source_sentence: The undoped NiCrAl alloy exhibits a continuous and significant weight loss, indicating poor scale adherence and spallation.

entities.name: MCrAlX alloys
entities.description: High-temperature alloy system (where M = Ni, Co, or Fe) used in oxidation-resistant coatings, tested at 1100 °C for 100 hours with varying dopant levels to evaluate oxidation and spallation behavior.

entities.name: Dopant level
entities.description: Concentration of additive element (e.g., reactive element dopant such as Y, Hf, or Zr) in weight percent (wt%), varied to study its influence on oxide scale adhesion and growth kinetics; optimal level around 0.1 wt% minimizes weight change.

entities.name: Specimen weight change
entities.description: Net mass change per unit area (mg/cm²) after 100 h exposure at 1100 °C, reflecting oxidation (positive weight gain) and spallation (negative contribution due to scale loss); exhibits U-shaped dependence on dopant level with minimum near 0.1 wt%.

entities.name: Total weight change
entities.description: Cumulative mass change (mg/cm²) including contributions from oxide growth and spallation losses; used interchangeably with specimen weight change in this schematic to assess coating durability.

entities.name: Isothermal condition
entities.description: Oxidation test conducted at constant 1100 °C for 100 h without thermal cycling; shows modest U-shaped weight change response to dopant level, indicating limited spallation.

entities.name: Cyclic condition
entities.description: Thermally cycled oxidation test at 1100 °C for 100 h involving repeated heating and cooling; exhibits a pronounced U-shaped weight change due to significant spallation, especially at non-optimal dopant levels.

entities.name: Non-adherent slow growth
entities.description: Regime I at low dopant levels (<0.05 wt%) where oxide scale forms slowly but lacks adhesion, leading to spallation and higher net weight change, especially under cyclic conditions.

entities.name: Adherent slow growth
entities.description: Regime II near 0.1 wt% dopant where oxide scale is both slow-growing and well-adhered, minimizing weight change and spallation—optimal for coating performance.

entities.name: Adherent excessive growth
entities.description: Regime III at high dopant levels (>0.2 wt%) where oxide scale remains adherent but grows excessively, increasing weight gain despite good adhesion.

entities.name: Spallation
entities.description: Loss of protective oxide scale due to poor adhesion or thermal stress, quantified indirectly via reduced net weight gain in cyclic tests; most severe at low and high dopant extremes, minimized near 0.1 wt%.

entities.name: Optimal dopant level
entities.description: Approximately 0.1 wt% additive concentration that minimizes specimen weight change by balancing oxide growth rate and scale adhesion, corresponding to Regime II (adherent slow growth).

entities.name: CMSX-4 superalloy

entities.name: Uncoated CMSX-4

entities.name: Ni–8Co–12Cr–7Al–Y

entities.name: Thermal mechanical fatigue (TMF) - out-of-phase

entities.name: Protective oxide scale

entities.name: Ni-Cr-Al-Y/ZrO2–6.1 wt%Y2O3 TBC system
entities.description: Thermal barrier coating (TBC) system composed of a Ni-Cr-Al-Y bond coat and a ZrO2–6.1 wt%Y2O3 top coat, tested under cyclic oxidation at 1100 °C. Performance is highly sensitive to Al and Y concentrations in the bond coat.

entities.name: Aluminium concentration
entities.description: Al content in the Ni-Cr-Al-Y bond coat, varied from 5.9 to 18.5 wt%. Higher Al concentrations (e.g., 18.5Al) correlate with accelerated oxidation (increased specific weight gain) and drastically reduced TBC life in cyclic testing at 1100 °C.

entities.name: Yttrium concentration
entities.description: Y content in the Ni-Cr-Al-Y bond coat, tested between 0.14 and 1.35 wt%. Both very low (0.14Y) and very high (1.35Y) Y levels lead to faster oxidation and shorter TBC life, while intermediate levels (0.22Y–0.95Y) yield better oxidation resistance and longer life, indicating an optimal Y range.

entities.name: Specific weight gain
entities.description: Measure of oxidation rate, expressed as mass gain per unit area during cyclic oxidation at 1100 °C. Higher values indicate faster scale formation and degradation. Ranges observed correlate strongly with Al and Y concentrations in the bond coat.

entities.name: Cycles to failure
entities.description: Number of thermal cycles (1100 °C max) until TBC failure, used as a metric for coating lifetime. Inversely correlated with specific weight gain: higher oxidation rates lead to fewer cycles to failure.

entities.name: Optimal yttrium concentration range
entities.description: Intermediate yttrium levels (0.22–0.95 wt%) in the Ni-Cr-Al-Y bond coat that minimize specific weight gain and maximize TBC life during cyclic oxidation at 1100 °C, as evidenced by slower oxidation kinetics and extended cycles to failure.

entities.name: High aluminium concentration (18.5Al)
entities.description: Bond coat with 18.5 wt% Al (Ni-35.7Cr-18.5Al-0.80Y) that exhibits the highest oxidation rate (specific weight gain) and shortest TBC life among tested compositions under cyclic 1100 °C exposure.

entities.name: Extreme yttrium concentrations
entities.description: Bond coats with either very low (0.14Y) or very high (1.35Y) yttrium content, both showing accelerated oxidation (high specific weight gain) and reduced TBC life compared to intermediate Y levels.

entities.name: Specific fuel consumption
entities.description: A performance metric for aeroengines indicating fuel efficiency, showing a steady decrease from approximately 1.2 to 0.55 lb/(h lb) between 1950 and 2000, reflecting significant improvements in Rolls-Royce engine efficiency over time.

entities.name: Take-off thrust
entities.description: The maximum thrust produced by an engine at take-off, which increased dramatically for Rolls-Royce large civil aeroengines from under 10,000 lb to 90,000 lb between 1950 and 2000, with accelerated growth after 1970 due to advancements in engine design and materials.

entities.name: Engine weight / take-off thrust
