entities.name: Single-crystal superalloys
entities.description: High-performance nickel-based superalloys used in high-pressure turbine blades, evolving through multiple generations from 1955 to 2005 with systematic compositional changes to enhance high-temperature strength and oxidation resistance.

entities.name: Chromium (Cr)
entities.description: Chromium content in single-crystal superalloys decreased significantly from approximately 18 wt% in early conventionally cast alloys to about 4 wt% by 2005, reflecting reduced reliance on Cr for oxidation resistance in favor of Al.

entities.name: Cobalt (Co)
entities.description: Cobalt is consistently present across alloy generations with fluctuating concentrations, typically maintained between 5–12 wt%, used to stabilize the microstructure and reduce diffusion rates.

entities.name: Tantalum + Tungsten (Ta+W)
entities.description: Combined refractory elements Ta and W introduced to strengthen the γ' phase; their total concentration varies across generations, generally increasing in second and third generations before slight adjustments in fourth-generation alloys.

entities.name: Molybdenum (Mo)
entities.description: Molybdenum content introduced in early single-crystal alloys as a solid-solution strengthener, with concentrations adjusted across generations, typically ranging from 0.5 to 2 wt%.

entities.name: Titanium (Ti)
entities.description: Titanium content was present in early alloys but decreased steadily to near zero by 2005, as Al became the primary γ' phase former, reducing the need for Ti.

entities.name: Aluminum (Al)
entities.description: Aluminum content shows a steady increase from ~5 wt% to over 6 wt% by 2005, serving as the primary γ' phase former and enhancing oxidation resistance, replacing Cr in modern alloys.

entities.name: Rhenium (Re)
entities.description: Rhenium appears in second-generation and later alloys, with concentrations rising to ~3–6 wt% in third-generation alloys, significantly improving creep resistance through solid-solution strengthening.

entities.name: Ruthenium (Ru)
entities.description: Ruthenium is introduced in fourth-generation single-crystal superalloys (~2000–2005) at ~3–6 wt%, added to suppress topologically close-packed (TCP) phase formation and enhance high-temperature stability.

entities.name: Year
entities.description: Time axis spanning from 1955 to 2005, marking the historical development of superalloy generations from conventionally cast to fourth-generation single-crystal variants.

entities.name: Composition (wt%)
entities.description: Weight percentage of alloying elements, used to quantify elemental concentrations in single-crystal superalloys across development generations.

entities.name: Fourth-generation superalloys
entities.description: Latest alloy generation (circa 2000–2005) characterized by inclusion of Ru, reduced Cr and Ti, elevated Al, and optimized refractory metals (Re, Ta, W) for maximum high-temperature performance.

entities.name: Third-generation superalloys
entities.description: Alloy generation (1990s–early 2000s) featuring high Re content (up to 6 wt%), low Cr, near-zero Ti, and increased Al, optimized for creep resistance.

entities.name: Second-generation superalloys
entities.description: Alloy generation (1980s–1990s) introducing Re and maintaining moderate levels of Co, Cr, and Al, with declining Ti.

entities.name: First-generation superalloys
entities.description: Early single-crystal alloys (1970s–1980s) with moderate Cr, Co, Al, and Ti, and initial use of Ta and Mo, but no Re or Ru.

entities.name: Conventionally cast superalloys
entities.description: Pre-single-crystal alloys (pre-1970s) with high Cr (~18 wt%), significant Ti, lower Al, and no Re or Ru, representing the baseline for compositional evolution.

entities.name: Thermal Barrier Coating (TBC)
entities.description: A multilayer coating system applied to metallic surfaces for thermal protection; its failure modes depend on top coat thickness (h) and elastic modulus ratio (E||/E⊥), with performance degrading as TGO thickness increases.

entities.name: Top coating thickness
entities.description: Thickness of the top ceramic layer in the TBC system, denoted as h, ranging across micrometers; lower values favor buckling failure, higher values promote edge delamination, with an intermediate 'fail-safe' range.

entities.name: Modulus ratio (E||/E⊥)
entities.description: Ratio of in-plane to through-thickness elastic moduli of the TBC; low values combined with thin coatings lead to buckling, while high values with thick coatings cause edge delamination.

entities.name: Thermally Grown Oxide (TGO)
entities.description: Oxide layer (typically Al2O3) formed at the bond coat–top coat interface during high-temperature exposure; its thickness critically influences TBC stability—1 µm allows a larger fail-safe zone, while 5 µm significantly reduces it.

entities.name: TGO thickness = 1 µm
entities.description: Condition representing a relatively thin thermally grown oxide layer; under this condition, the fail-safe region in the failure map is larger, indicating greater operational stability.

entities.name: TGO thickness = 5 µm
entities.description: Condition representing a thick thermally grown oxide layer; this reduces the fail-safe region in the failure map, increasing susceptibility to both buckling and edge delamination.

entities.name: Buckling failure region
entities.description: Region in the failure map characterized by low top coat thickness (h) and low modulus ratio (E||/E⊥), where compressive stresses cause coating buckling.

entities.name: Edge delamination region
entities.description: Region in the failure map at high h and high E||/E⊥ where interfacial stresses exceed fracture toughness, leading to delamination initiating at coating edges.

entities.name: Fail-safe region
entities.description: Intermediate zone in the failure map where neither buckling nor edge delamination occurs; its size is inversely correlated with TGO thickness.

entities.name: Mode II interfacial fracture toughness (ΓII)
entities.description: Critical energy release rate for shear-mode (mode II) interfacial cracking; higher ΓII expands the fail-safe region by resisting edge delamination.

entities.name: Characteristic delamination width (b)
entities.description: Length scale representing the width of an edge-initiated delamination; influences the boundary between fail-safe and edge delamination regions.

relationships.description: As TGO thickness increases from 1 µm to 5 µm, the fail-safe region shrinks, indicating reduced operational stability.
relationships.source_sentence: Comparing (a) and (b) shows that a thicker TGO shrinks the fail-safe region, making the coating more prone to failure.

entities.name: Diamond cubic
entities.description: Material class with the lowest melting point diffusivity among all crystal classes shown, below 10^-15 m²/s, indicating excellent resistance to atomic diffusion and creep at high temperatures.

entities.name: FCC metals
entities.description: Face-centered cubic metals exhibit low melting point diffusivity in the range of 10^-13 to 10^-12 m²/s, suggesting moderate resistance to high-temperature diffusion-driven deformation.

entities.name: BCC transition metals
entities.description: Body-centered cubic transition metals show the highest melting point diffusivities among the classes, ranging from 10^-12 to 10^-9 m²/s, indicating significant atomic mobility at melting and poor creep resistance.

entities.name: BCC rare earth
entities.description: Body-centered cubic rare earth elements exhibit very high melting point diffusivity, spanning 10^-12 to 10^-9 m²/s, comparable to BCC transition metals, implying high atomic mobility near melting.

entities.name: Melting point diffusivity
entities.description: Diffusion coefficient measured at the material’s melting point, used as an indicator of high-temperature atomic mobility; lower values correlate with better creep resistance in structural materials.

entities.name: Ice
entities.description: Crystalline water (ice) shows low melting point diffusivity, positioned near diamond cubic materials on the logarithmic scale, though exact value not specified; implies limited self-diffusion at 0°C.

entities.name: Trigonal
entities.description: Materials with trigonal crystal structure exhibit low melting point diffusivity, grouped among the lower-diffusivity classes, though precise range not quantified in the chart.

entities.name: Oxide
entities.description: Oxide materials display relatively low melting point diffusivity, consistent with ceramic behavior and good high-temperature stability.

entities.name: Indium
entities.description: Indium, a post-transition metal, shows moderate melting point diffusivity, positioned between low-diffusivity ceramics and high-diffusivity BCC metals.

entities.name: Alkali halides
entities.description: Ionic compounds like NaCl exhibit low to moderate melting point diffusivity, reflecting limited ion mobility at melting compared to metallic BCC systems.

entities.name: Graphite
entities.description: Layered carbon structure with anisotropic diffusion; shown to have relatively low melting point diffusivity in this context, likely reflecting in-plane or average behavior.

entities.name: HCP
entities.description: Hexagonal close-packed metals exhibit moderate melting point diffusivity, higher than FCC metals but significantly lower than BCC transition metals.

entities.name: Metal carbides
entities.description: Refractory compounds with strong covalent/metallic bonding, showing low melting point diffusivity, consistent with their use in high-temperature applications.

entities.name: BCC alkali
entities.description: Alkali metals with body-centered cubic structure show elevated melting point diffusivity compared to ceramics and FCC metals, but generally lower than BCC transition metals and rare earths.

entities.name: BCC alkali metals

entities.name: FCC metals
entities.description: Face-centered cubic metals with normalised activation energy for diffusion in the range of 18–19, moderately higher than BCC metals, indicating improved but not exceptional creep resistance.

entities.name: Diamond cubic
entities.description: Materials with diamond cubic crystal structure (e.g., diamond, silicon) exhibiting the highest normalised activation energy for diffusion, above 30, which correlates with excellent creep resistance due to strong covalent bonding and low diffusivity.

entities.name: Normalised activation energy for diffusion
entities.description: Dimensionless quantity Qv/(RTm) representing the energy barrier for atomic diffusion normalised by the product of gas constant and melting temperature; higher values indicate greater resistance to diffusion and improved high-temperature stability.

entities.name: Creep resistance
entities.description: Material’s ability to resist deformation under sustained stress at high temperatures; positively correlated with normalised activation energy for diffusion as indicated in the trend description.

entities.name: HCP
entities.description: Hexagonal close-packed metals with intermediate normalised activation energy for diffusion, positioned between BCC metals and FCC metals in the chart, suggesting moderate diffusivity and creep resistance.

entities.name: BCC transition
entities.description: Body-centered cubic transition metals with normalised activation energy slightly higher than alkali and rare earth BCC metals, likely in the range of 16–17, reflecting stronger bonding and better high-temperature performance.

entities.name: Graphite
entities.description: Layered hexagonal carbon structure with relatively low normalised activation energy for diffusion due to anisotropic bonding, likely in the mid-range (~20), indicating moderate diffusivity perpendicular to basal planes.

entities.name: Tetragonal
entities.description: Materials with tetragonal crystal structure exhibiting normalised activation energy above FCC metals but below covalent network solids, likely in the 22–25 range, indicating reduced diffusivity compared to close-packed metals.

entities.name: Alkali halides
entities.description: Ionic compounds (e.g., NaCl) with normalised activation energy in the 20–24 range, reflecting moderate diffusion barriers governed by ionic bonding and defect mechanisms.

entities.name: Oxides
entities.description: Ceramic oxides with relatively high normalised activation energy (25–28), due to strong ionic/covalent bonds, resulting in low diffusivity and good high-temperature stability.

entities.name: Carbides
entities.description: Refractory carbides (e.g., TiC, SiC) with high normalised activation energy (~28–30), reflecting strong covalent/ionic bonding and excellent resistance to diffusion and creep.

entities.name: Ice
entities.description: Crystalline water (H2O) with relatively low normalised activation energy despite hydrogen bonding, likely around 18–20, due to its low melting point and high defect mobility.

entities.name: Trigonal
entities.description: Materials with trigonal crystal symmetry (e.g., calcite, quartz) exhibiting moderate to high normalised activation energy, likely 24–27, due to directional bonding and structural complexity.

entities.name: Olivine
entities.description: Nesosilicate mineral with orthorhombic structure (grouped under crystal classes here) showing high normalised activation energy (~27–29), consistent with silicate network rigidity and low cation diffusivity.

entities.name: Ni3(Al, Ta)
entities.description: Polycrystalline intermetallic alloy composed of nickel, aluminum, and tantalum, studied for its internal friction behavior across temperatures from 900 K to 1025 K.

entities.name: Internal Friction (IF)
entities.description: A measure of energy dissipation in the material, observed as a peak in IF × 10³ that shifts to higher frequencies with increasing temperature (900–1025 K), indicating thermally activated relaxation processes.

entities.name: Frequency
entities.description: Oscillation frequency (in Hz) at which internal friction is measured; the peak IF occurs at a characteristic frequency that increases with temperature from 900 K to 1025 K.

entities.name: Temperature
entities.description: Measurement temperatures ranging from 900 K to 1025 K; higher temperatures shift the IF peak to higher frequencies, reflecting enhanced atomic mobility.

entities.name: ln ω
entities.description: Natural logarithm of angular frequency (ω = 2πf), used in the Arrhenius plot to linearize the thermally activated relaxation behavior.

entities.name: 1000/Tp
entities.description: Inverse of peak temperature (Tp) scaled by 1000, used as the x-axis in the Arrhenius plot; lower values correspond to higher temperatures (900–1025 K).

entities.name: Activation Energy (Hact)
entities.description: Energy barrier for the relaxation process responsible for internal friction, quantified as 290 kJ/mol from the slope of the Arrhenius plot.

entities.name: IF Peak Frequency Shift
entities.description: Systematic increase in the frequency at which internal friction peaks as temperature rises from 900 K to 1025 K, indicating a thermally activated relaxation mechanism.

entities.name: Linear Arrhenius Behavior
entities.description: Straight-line relationship in the Arrhenius plot (ln ω vs. 1000/Tp) with negative slope, confirming a single dominant thermally activated process with activation energy of 290 kJ/mol.

relationships.description: As temperature increases from 900 K to 1025 K, the peak frequency of internal friction shifts to higher values, indicating faster relaxation kinetics.
relationships.source_sentence: At each temperature, a peak in IF occurs at a specific frequency, and this peak frequency shifts to higher values as the temperature increases from 900 K to 1025 K.

relationships.description: Temperature influences the internal friction response by shifting the peak position in frequency, though the IF magnitude trend is not quantified; the primary effect is on relaxation rate.
relationships.source_sentence: At each temperature, a peak in IF occurs at a specific frequency, and this peak frequency shifts to higher values as the temperature increases.

relationships.description: ln ω decreases linearly with increasing 1000/Tp (i.e., decreasing temperature), forming a straight line in the Arrhenius plot used to extract activation energy.
relationships.source_sentence: Chart (b) is an Arrhenius plot of the natural logarithm of the angular frequency (ln ω) versus the inverse of the peak temperature (1000/Tp). The data points form a straight line with a negative slope.

relationships.description: The linear Arrhenius behavior directly enables the determination of the activation energy as 290 kJ/mol from the slope of the ln ω vs. 1000/Tp plot.
relationships.source_sentence: The data points form a straight line with a negative slope, from which an activation energy Hact of 290 kJ/mol is deduced.

entities.name: Ni-Al single crystals
entities.description: Nickel-aluminum single crystals with varying aluminum content (12.2% to 16.1%) and aged at 600–625°C, used to study ordering hardening behavior under room-temperature compression.

entities.name: Ordering hardening (Δτ)
entities.description: The increase in shear stress due to ordering hardening in Ni-Al single crystals, ranging from 0 to ~160 MN/m², which increases linearly with the microstructural parameter (rf/T)¹/², confirming theoretical models for weakly coupled dislocations.

entities.name: (rf/T)¹/²
entities.description: A dimensionless microstructural parameter combining mean particle radius (r), volume fraction of ordered precipitates (f), and dislocation line tension (T); ranges from 0 to ~1.7 (m/N)¹/² and linearly correlates with ordering hardening Δτ.

entities.name: Aluminum content
entities.description: Aluminum concentration in Ni-Al single crystals, varied between 12.2% and 16.1% across experimental conditions, influencing precipitate formation and thus ordering hardening.

entities.name: Ageing temperature
entities.description: Heat treatment temperature (600°C or 625°C) applied to Ni-Al single crystals to promote ordering and precipitate formation, affecting the values of r and f in the (rf/T)¹/² parameter.

entities.name: Linear trend between Δτ and (rf/T)¹/²
entities.description: Observed linear correlation where ordering hardening (Δτ) increases proportionally with (rf/T)¹/² from 0 to 160 MN/m² over a (rf/T)¹/² range of 0–1.7 (m/N)¹/², validating theoretical predictions for weakly coupled dislocations.

relationships.description: Ordering hardening (Δτ) increases linearly with the microstructural parameter (rf/T)¹/², rising from 0 to ~160 MN/m² as (rf/T)¹/² increases from 0 to ~1.7 (m/N)¹/².
relationships.source_sentence: The ordering hardening increases linearly from 0 to about 160 MN/m² as (rf/T)¹/² increases from 0 to approximately 1.7 (m/N)¹/².

relationships.description: Aluminum content influences precipitate volume fraction (f) and possibly radius (r), thereby affecting the (rf/T)¹/² parameter used to normalize ordering hardening.
relationships.source_sentence: Data points from tests on Ni-Al single crystals with different compositions... show a clear linear relationship.

relationships.description: Ageing temperature controls precipitate size (r) and volume fraction (f), which directly determine the value of (rf/T)¹/².
relationships.source_sentence: Data points from tests on Ni-Al single crystals with... different ageing temperatures... show a clear linear relationship.

relationships.description: The linear trend confirms that Δτ is quantitatively governed by (rf/T)¹/², supporting dislocation theory for weakly coupled systems.
relationships.source_sentence: This confirms the theoretical prediction for weakly coupled dislocations.

entities.name: Ordered γ' Particle
entities.description: Ordered intermetallic precipitate phase γ' being sheared by dislocation pairs; appears as a circular or spherical obstacle in both subfigures (a) and (b).

attributes.function: Obstacle to dislocation motion; its interaction with dislocation pairs defines coupling strength.

entities.name: Dislocation 1
entities.description: First dislocation in the shearing pair, labeled (1), moving through the material and interacting with the γ' particle.

attributes.position: Approaching or passing through γ' particle from left in both (a) and (b)
attributes.function: Carries plastic deformation; part of a dislocation pair shearing the γ' precipitate.

entities.name: Dislocation 2
entities.description: Second dislocation in the shearing pair, labeled (2), following dislocation 1 and interacting with the same γ' particle.

attributes.position: Trailing dislocation, right of dislocation 1 in both (a) and (b)
attributes.function: Completes the shearing process initiated by dislocation 1; spacing relative to dislocation 1 determines coupling strength.

entities.name: Weak Pair-Coupling Configuration
entities.description: Subfigure (a) showing dislocations spaced far apart relative to the γ' particle diameter, indicating weak interaction between the dislocation pair.

attributes.function: Illustrates mechanical response under weak dislocation coupling.

entities.name: Strong Pair-Coupling Configuration
entities.description: Subfigure (b) showing dislocations closely spaced, with separation comparable to γ' particle diameter, indicating strong coupling.

attributes.function: Illustrates mechanical response under strong dislocation coupling.

entities.name: Applied Shear Stress
entities.description: External shear stress τ driving dislocation motion and particle shearing in both configurations.

attributes.function: Drives dislocation glide and determines shearing mechanism.
